alignment.note: Greek uses the imperfect ἐζήτουν ('they were seeking') as a single synthetic verb form, matched by Latin imperfect quærebant. Syriac ܘܒܥܝܢ ܗܘܘ employs the analytic periphrastic construction (active participle + enclitic ܗܘܘ) to express durative past, a standard Syriac equivalent for the Greek imperfect.

The Greek object pronoun αὐτόν and Latin eum stand as separate accusative pronouns, whereas Syriac incorporates the object as the pronominal suffix on the infinitive ܠܡܐܚܕܗ ('to seize-him'). The pronominal reference is preserved but morphologically fused into the verb.

Greek ἐφοβήθησαν and Latin timuerunt govern a direct accusative object ('feared the crowd'), while Syriac ܘܕܚܠܘ ܡܢ uses the verb of fearing with the preposition ܡܢ ('feared from/of the people'), a typical Aramaic construction for the object of fear; the conjunction and verb are conflated in the single Syriac form ܘܕܚܠܘ.

Greek ὄχλον, Latin turbam, and Syriac ܥܡܐ all denote the crowd; the Syriac root e-m-m carries a slightly more ethnic-collective nuance ('the people') than the neutral Greek/Latin 'crowd', but the referent is identical.

Greek ὅτι and Latin quoniam introduce the indirect statement as explicit complementizers. Syriac dispenses with a separate conjunction, instead prefixing the relative/complementizing particle ܕ directly onto ܕܥܠܝܗܘܢ, so the subordinating function is morphologically absorbed rather than lexically separate.

Greek πρὸς αὐτούς and Latin ad eos render the prepositional phrase with separate preposition and pronoun, whereas Syriac ܕܥܠܝܗܘܢ fuses the relative particle, preposition ܥܠ, and the 3mp suffix into one word; the meaning 'against/concerning them' is equivalent.

Greek places the verb εἶπεν after the article+noun παραβολήν (with no demonstrative), Latin adds the demonstrative hanc following parabolam, and Syriac likewise supplies the demonstrative ܗܢܐ after ܡܬܠܐ. Both Syriac and Latin make the parable definite/deictic ('this parable') where the Greek uses only the article.

Greek uses the aorist participle ἀφέντες αὐτόν ('having left him') and Latin the ablative absolute relicto eo, both circumstantial constructions; Syriac employs a finite coordinate verb with object suffix ܘܫܒܩܘܗܝ ('and they left-him'), paratactic rather than participial.
